paras: The attempted lynching of John Haynes took place in December 1903, when mobs twice tried to take Haynes, a sixteen-year-old Black youth accused of attempted assault, from jail in Madison County, Tennessee. Early on December 6 a crowd of 'men and boys' tried to break into the county jail at Jackson but was turned back by the sheriff and dispersed by police, and days later a mob broke open the jail at Henderson but did not find him. Haynes was later tried at Jackson and sentenced to twenty-one years in the penitentiary.

Haynes was accused of attempting to assault Miss Daisy McMahon near Malesus, in Madison County. The December dispatches placed the alleged offense on Saturday, December 5, while a March 1904 report gave December 4. He was held in the county jail at Jackson.

Before dawn on December 6 a mob of 'men and boys' gathered at the jail intending to take Haynes out 'to lynch him', and tried to break in the north door. According to the Jackson special printed in the Union City Commercial, Sheriff R. C. Mayo refused to give up the prisoner and asked the crowd to desist because his daughter was 'very low with fever' and excitement might kill her. Most of the crowd sympathized with him, but 'a large number' wanted to push through, and the police chief and several policemen then arrived and dispersed it.

Haynes was then moved out of the Jackson jail to prevent mob violence. A Jackson dispatch dated December 9 reported that a mob had broken open the jail at Henderson 'at an early hour' in search of him. On word of the mob's intention to go to Henderson, Haynes had been 'again spirited away', and his whereabouts were reported unknown.

In March 1904 Haynes was brought from the jail at Trenton to Jackson, tried at once, 'submitted his case', and was sentenced to twenty-one years. The sheriff left immediately for the penitentiary with him 'to escape another probable outbreak among the people'. No report of arrests of members of either mob appears in the coverage.

Coverage came from white papers in Tennessee and Kentucky, beginning with a short Jackson dispatch in the Paducah Sun on December 7 headlined 'Failed to Get Prisoner'. The Union City Commercial printed a fuller Jackson special on December 11 under the headline 'Sheriff's Plea Halted the Mob', crediting the sheriff's personal appeal for turning the crowd. Both papers described the attempted assault as something Haynes 'committed' or was 'charged with', and the Paducah Sun ended its report of the Henderson break-in with the line 'It will go hard with the negro if he is found.'

The sentencing ran in March 1904 in Mrs. Grundy of Tracy City, the Lawrence Democrat and the Bolivar Bulletin under the headline 'Long Sentence for a Bruite'. No Black-press coverage of the episode was found.
The Commercial named Sheriff R. C. Mayo as the officer who refused the mob, while the Paducah Sun credited 'the jailer'; both told the same story of an ill daughter, which suggests one officer.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of John Haynes
bases: Mobs twice sought to take John Haynes from jail 'to lynch him' (A4) and broke open a second jail in search of him (A2, A3); he was not taken, so this is an attempted lynching.

A mob of 'men and boys' sought Haynes to lynch him for an alleged attempted assault (A4), but he was not killed; he was later tried and sentenced to 21 years (A5), so this was an attempt, not a completed lynching.

The Paducah Sun's Jackson dispatch (A1) and the Jackson special printed in the Union City Commercial (A4) agree on the Dec. 6 jail siege, and a March 1904 item (A5) independently says Haynes 'twice escaped a mob'; both December reports may share a Jackson source.

accounts.label: Jackson wire (Paducah Sun)
accounts.gist: 'The jailer' told the mob his daughter was ill and might die from excitement, and police dispersed the mob before it could force its way in.

accounts.label: Jackson wire, second attempt
accounts.gist: A mob broke open the Henderson jail looking for Haynes, who had been moved from Jackson and then 'again spirited away'.

accounts.label: Sentencing report
accounts.gist: Haynes, who 'twice escaped a mob', was brought from Trenton to Jackson, tried, sentenced to 21 years and taken at once to the penitentiary.

framing.detail: Reports took the accusation as fact ('the attempted assault he committed') while crediting the sheriff's plea under the headline 'Sheriff's Plea Halted the Mob'.
The Paducah Sun closed its Dec. 9 item with 'It will go hard with the negro if he is found', and the 1904 sentencing item was headlined 'Long Sentence for a Bruite'.
